:question/math-academy-id "q-76334" :question/problem "The vectors ${a}_{1},$ ${a}_{2},$ ${a}_{3},$ and ${a}_{4}$ are given below. Determine whether $B={{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}}.$ If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3},$ where ${a}_{4}={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}.$

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{4}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 4 \\ -22\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "We want to determine if $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}}.$ So, we want to find ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}\in R$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+{x}_{2}{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}+{x}_{3}{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}={{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 4 \\ -22\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{4}}.
$$

This equation is equivalent to the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=-4 \\ -{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=4 \\ 4{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}+5{x}_{3}=-22\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & -4 \\ -1 & 1 & -1 & 4 \\ 4 & -4 & 5 & -22\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & 5 & -22\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 1 & -6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+4{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the reduced matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, and $3$rd columns. So,  $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}}.$
Also, the matrix tells us that ${x}_{1}=2,$ ${x}_{2}=0,$ and ${x}_{3}=-6,$ meaning that

$$
2\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+0\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}+(-6)\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}={{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 4 \\ -22\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{4}}.
$$

Therefore, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=2+0+(-6)=-4.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-55d04c6b-2631-5950-abad-871e8e80ece8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-55d04c6b-2631-5950-abad-871e8e80ece8" :answer-field/id #uuid "55d04c6b-2631-5950-abad-871e8e80ece8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-f568bc4f-3c69-5e10-af38-07fcd1985ab1" :answer-field/choices ["answer-5aaf6733-e757-5737-a6d7-d37f344e2387" "answer-f568bc4f-3c69-5e10-af38-07fcd1985ab1" "answer-fed87abb-5218-5d71-9132-58acdc6b2500" "answer-6536472f-623b-557c-ba85-a0b19e98cf60" "answer-a2ba4765-28ed-5cc7-822f-5b6db17d805d"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5aaf6733-e757-5737-a6d7-d37f344e2387" :answer/id #uuid "5aaf6733-e757-5737-a6d7-d37f344e2387" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-12" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f568bc4f-3c69-5e10-af38-07fcd1985ab1" :answer/id #uuid "f568bc4f-3c69-5e10-af38-07fcd1985ab1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fed87abb-5218-5d71-9132-58acdc6b2500" :answer/id #uuid "fed87abb-5218-5d71-9132-58acdc6b2500" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6536472f-623b-557c-ba85-a0b19e98cf60" :answer/id #uuid "6536472f-623b-557c-ba85-a0b19e98cf60" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a2ba4765-28ed-5cc7-822f-5b6db17d805d" :answer/id #uuid "a2ba4765-28ed-5cc7-822f-5b6db17d805d" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "${{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}}$ is not a basis of $\text{Span}{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}}$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121040 :tutorial/content "A **basis** of a subspace $U$ (in $\mathbb{R}^n$) is a set of vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that is linearly independent and spans $U.$

For example, consider the following subspace consisting of the span of three vectors:
![](images/aa/aaa76e82d8d54b305cfcfb0414f1fe7dd4d1c9d3ff932b4206a7b864922b394e.svg)

To find a basis of $U,$ we need to find a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $U.$

**Watch out!** The set
![](images/23/237305d1b82f44e0c365f721a33c35d8d983bd5facd4471d1885e8180ec7267e.svg)
is *not* a basis of $U.$ It's true that this set *spans* $U,$ but the vectors in this set are *not* linearly independent. In particular, the vector $\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3$ can be written as a linear combination of $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2$ as follows:

![](images/1d/1d0ff277adbace09315a1c0cd7c964eac41f5e2f080d0e32f888f379be435da0.svg)

To find a basis of $U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \},$ we can start with $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \},$ but we need to remove any "redundant" vectors that can be written as a linear combination of other vectors in the set. In this case, we remove ${\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3}$ because it can be written as a linear combination of $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}.$

We are left with the set

![](images/79/79c529aa2fb5373ff9f8798300b1423ea63f90778bd4832ba1276f6af9c21f04.svg)

These two vectors are linearly independent (since they are not parallel), and removing a redundant vector does not change the span, so these vectors still span $U.$ That is to say,

$$
U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \} = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}.
$$

Therefore, the set $\mathcal{B} = \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ is a basis of $U.$

**Note:** To see that the vectors $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ still span $U,$ first note that any vector $\mathbf{b} \in U$ can be written as a linear combination of the three original vectors:

$$
\mathbf{b} = x_1 {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1} + x_2 {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} + x_3 {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3}
$$

Since ${\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} = -{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}+3{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2},$ then we must have 

$$

$$

17592186120688 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121040 :tutorial/content "A **basis** of a subspace $U$ (in $\mathbb{R}^n$) is a set of vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that is linearly independent and spans $U.$

For example, consider the following subspace consisting of the span of three vectors:

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

To find a basis of $U,$ we need to find a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $U.$

**Watch out!** The set
$[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
is *not* a basis of $U.$ It's true that this set *spans* $U,$ but the vectors in this set are *not* linearly independent. In particular, the vector $\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3$ can be written as a linear combination of $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

To find a basis of $U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \},$ we can start with $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \},$ but we need to remove any "redundant" vectors that can be written as a linear combination of other vectors in the set. In this case, we remove ${\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3}$ because it can be written as a linear combination of $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}.$

We are left with the set

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

These two vectors are linearly independent (since they are not parallel), and removing a redundant vector does not change the span, so these vectors still span $U.$ That is to say,

$$
U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \} = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}.
$$

Therefore, the set $\mathcal{B} = \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ is a basis of $U.$

**Note:** To see that the vectors $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ still span $U,$ first note that any vector $\mathbf{b} \in U$ can be written as a linear combination of the three original vectors:

$$
\mathbf{b} = x_1 {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1} + x_2 {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} + x_3 {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3}
$$

Since ${\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} = -{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}+3{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2},$ then we must have 

$$
\begin{aligned}b & ={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}(-{a}_{1}+3{a}_{2}) \\  & =({x}_{1}-{x}_{3}){a}_{1}+({x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}){a}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

which shows that $\mathbf{b}$ can actually be written as a linear combination of only two vectors, ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}.$

Therefore, we can conclude that the set $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ spans the subspace $U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4ff21f5d-5007-5b74-b135-bdb080fd5541" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3206 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "be88e95e-9faa-5bfe-b721-4eda45231dc0" :step/math-academy-id 17504 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120689}} {:db/id 17592186120689 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119815 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119626 :question/id #uuid "51c289e1-f118-5444-bf1d-c7e8262c549f" :question/math-academy-id "e-4816"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f892805c-2c2c-5105-91ba-353aefe7b7f2" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050426}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120517} {:db/id 17592186120518} {:db/id 17592186247170} {:db/id 17592186345006} {:db/id 17592186345007} {:db/id 17592186399713} {:db/id 17592186399720}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Basis of the Space Spanned by a Set of Vectors Using Inspection"} :step/id #uuid "1169ef7f-a019-5cfa-8ef6-1d2ff514f2f1" :step/math-academy-id 17505 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120752}} {:db/id 17592186120752 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121064 :tutorial/content "In the previous example, it was easy to see that one vector was a linear combination of the others. But what can we do when it's not so easy to tell? For example, consider the subspace

$$

$$

To find a subset of linearly independent vectors, we can put the vectors in a matrix and compute the reduced row echelon form:

$$

$$
